title: bcrypt Hash Calculator: Cost vs Time 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate bcrypt hashing time by cost factor. See ms per hash, hashes/sec and GPU crack speed. OWASP-aligned recommendation for cost=12+ in 2026.
intro:
**bcrypt** is a password-hashing function designed by **Niels Provos and David Mazières** in 1999, originally for OpenBSD, and built on the Blowfish cipher key-schedule. Unlike fast cryptographic hashes such as MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256, bcrypt is **intentionally slow**: its **cost factor** (also called the **work factor**) controls exactly how slow it is, and how expensive it becomes for an attacker to brute-force a stolen hash database.

The cost factor is an **exponent of base 2**: `cost=N` means bcrypt performs `2^N` internal key-expansion rounds. So `cost=10` runs 1,024 rounds, `cost=12` runs 4,096 rounds, `cost=14` runs 16,384 rounds, and so on. **Each +1 in cost exactly doubles the hashing time**, both for legitimate logins on your server and for an attacker trying to crack the hash offline. The bcrypt specification allows costs from 4 to 31, but practical values for password hashing in 2026 are between 10 and 14.

On a modern server CPU (AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon, 2024-2026 generation), `cost=12` takes approximately **100 ms per hash** in single-threaded execution: fast enough for user logins (acceptable latency at scale) but slow enough to make brute-force attacks economically prohibitive on commodity GPU hardware. `cost=10` runs in ~12 ms and is now considered **insufficient** by **OWASP's 2025 Password Storage Cheat Sheet**, which sets the minimum recommended bcrypt cost at **12** for 2025-2026. `cost=14` (~400 ms) provides extra margin at some cost to UX. **Each +1 doubles the attacker's cost just as much as yours**.

bcrypt has three important properties beyond simple slowness: **(1) a built-in 128-bit random salt** per password, generated automatically and stored alongside the hash, which makes rainbow-table attacks computationally infeasible; **(2) modest memory hardness** — bcrypt's Blowfish key schedule needs ~4 KB of working state (the P-array and four 1-KB S-boxes), which **severely limits GPU and ASIC parallelism** compared to MD5; **(3) a known 72-byte truncation limit** on the input password, a quirk of the original spec that you must work around if your users have very long passphrases.

This calculator estimates the **wall-clock hashing time** at a given cost factor on a reference modern CPU, plus approximate **throughput in hashes per second** and a security recommendation tuned to 2026 hardware capabilities. Always benchmark on your **production hardware** before committing to a cost factor in production code: a MacBook Pro dev machine can be 5-10× faster than a t3.micro burstable VM under sustained load.
keyTakeaway: **Time per hash = base_time × 2^(cost − base_cost)**. At cost=10 ≈ 12 ms; cost=12 ≈ 100 ms (OWASP recommended minimum for 2025); cost=14 ≈ 400 ms. Each +1 to cost **doubles** the hashing time for both you and an attacker.
useCases: Backend engineer setting a secure bcrypt cost factor for a new SaaS user authentication system, ensuring logins take ~100-300 ms on the production cloud VM without degrading UX. The calc shows that cost=12 hits ~100 ms (OWASP minimum) and cost=13 hits ~200 ms.

Security team auditing a legacy PHP app using cost=8 (~0.8 ms, considered insecure since 2018) and quantifying the migration cost: rehashing 2 million stored hashes at cost=12 requires ~200,000 CPU-seconds, or ~55 hours on a single core, or ~7 hours parallelized across 8 cores.

Capacity planner for a high-traffic banking login endpoint estimating concurrent bcrypt verifications per server: at cost=12 (100 ms/hash) and 8 cores dedicated to auth, the theoretical ceiling is 80 logins/second; peak traffic of 50 logins/sec leaves comfortable headroom.

Pentester estimating attacker cracking speed on a 4× NVIDIA RTX 4090 rig (each card does ~5,250 bcrypt/s at cost=12, so 21,000/s total) against a stolen hash table; for an 8-char random alphanumeric password (62^8 combinations) the worst case is ~330 years and the average case is ~165 years.

DevOps engineer setting an opportunistic rehash policy: on successful login, if the stored hash is below cost=12, transparently rehash the plaintext at the new minimum cost and update the DB. The calc helps justify the chosen new minimum given current hardware.

Compliance auditor checking PCI-DSS requirement 8.3.2 ("render passwords unreadable using strong cryptography") for a payment processor: bcrypt cost=12 satisfies the spirit of the rule for 2025-2026; cost=10 raises an audit finding.

CTO of a startup evaluating Argon2id vs bcrypt for a new mobile-backend API: bcrypt is universally supported in Node.js, Python, Go, Ruby, Rust and PHP, has 25+ years of cryptanalysis with no practical breaks, and the calc shows cost=12 provides ~100 ms latency at acceptable cost, making it a pragmatic choice when Argon2id libraries are unavailable.

Embedded systems developer prototyping authentication for an ARM Cortex-A53 IoT device: the same cost=12 that runs in 100 ms on x86 takes 350-500 ms on the ARM SBC. The calc helps choose cost=10 (~50-70 ms on ARM) as a compromise between security and UX on lower-power hardware.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

bcrypt's cost factor is a base-2 exponent applied to the number of key-schedule iterations inside the Blowfish cipher. The wall-clock time scales **exponentially**:

```
Time(cost) = T_ref × 2^(cost − cost_ref)

Where:
  T_ref     = measured time (seconds) at a known reference cost on your hardware
  cost_ref  = the reference cost factor used to establish T_ref
  cost      = the target cost factor you want to evaluate

Example (commodity server CPU, 2024):
  T_ref = 0.012 s  at  cost_ref = 10
  Time(12) = 0.012 × 2^(12−10) = 0.012 × 4 = 0.048 s  ≈ 48 ms
  Time(14) = 0.012 × 2^(14−10) = 0.012 × 16 = 0.192 s ≈ 192 ms

Hashes per second:
  hashes_per_sec = 1 / Time(cost)
```

> **Note:** bcrypt is memory-hard in the sense that it requires ~4 KB of RAM per hash (the Blowfish P-array + S-boxes), which severely limits GPU parallelism compared to pure compute-bound hashes like MD5.

---

## Reference Table

Benchmarks collected from open-source projects (hashcat, john-the-ripper) and OWASP guidance. CPU column = single core of a modern server (e.g., AMD EPYC 7763); GPU = NVIDIA RTX 4090.

| Cost | Rounds (2^cost) | Time/hash (CPU) | CPU hashes/s | GPU hashes/s (RTX 4090) | Security rating (2025) |
|------|----------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| 8    | 256            | ~0.8 ms         | ~1,250       | ~350,000                 | ❌ Insecure            |
| 10   | 1,024          | ~12 ms          | ~83          | ~21,000                  | ⚠️ Marginal            |
| 11   | 2,048          | ~25 ms          | ~40          | ~10,500                  | ⚠️ Marginal            |
| 12   | 4,096          | ~100 ms         | ~10          | ~5,250                   | ✅ Recommended (2025)  |
| 13   | 8,192          | ~200 ms         | ~5           | ~2,625                   | ✅ Strong              |
| 14   | 16,384         | ~400 ms         | ~2.5         | ~1,312                   | ✅ Very strong         |
| 15   | 32,768         | ~800 ms         | ~1.25        | ~656                     | ⚠️ May impact UX       |

> GPU figures assume bcrypt's memory access pattern limits parallelism to ~1 hash per SM; actual throughput varies by driver and implementation.

---

## Typical Examples

**Example 1 — Startup web app (cost=12)**
A Node.js API uses `bcrypt.hash(password, 12)`. On their 2-core VPS (2× AMD EPYC core):
- Time per hash ≈ 100 ms → 10 hashes/s per core → 20 hashes/s total
- Peak login load = 5 requests/s → well within capacity, no queue buildup.
- An attacker with an RTX 4090 cracking offline: ~5,250 hashes/s. An 8-char random alphanumeric password (62^8 ≈ 2.18 × 10¹⁴ combinations) would take **~1.3 billion seconds (~41 years)** to exhaust at that rate.

**Example 2 — Legacy app rehash migration (cost=8 → cost=12)**
An e-commerce platform has 500,000 user records hashed at cost=8. Rehashing all at cost=12:
- Time per hash ≈ 100 ms × 500,000 = 50,000 s ≈ **13.9 hours** on a single CPU core.
- Solution: run a background job at login (rehash on successful auth), completing migration passively within weeks.

**Example 3 — High-traffic API (cost=14)**
A financial services app wants cost=14 (~400 ms). With 8 CPU cores dedicated to auth:
- Throughput = 8 × (1/0.4) = **20 hashes/s**. At peak 15 logins/s, a queue would form.
- Decision: drop to cost=13 (~200 ms) → 40 hashes/s, comfortable headroom at 15 logins/s.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Using cost=10 in 2025 and calling it "secure."** Cost=10 was OWASP's recommendation circa 2012. GPU hardware has improved ~10× since then. At cost=10, an RTX 4090 does ~21,000 hashes/s—a 6-char lowercase password is cracked in seconds. **Minimum: cost=12.**

2. **Confusing cost with the number of iterations directly.** The cost factor is an *exponent*: cost=12 means 2¹² = 4,096 rounds, NOT 12 rounds. Developers sometimes increase cost from 12 to 13 thinking it "adds 1 round"—it actually doubles the work.

3. **Benchmarking on a dev laptop and deploying to production.** A MacBook M3 hashes bcrypt at cost=12 in ~30 ms; a cloud t3.micro (burstable CPU) might take 250–400 ms under load. Always benchmark on production hardware.

4. **Ignoring the 72-character password limit.** bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes. A user with a 100-character passphrase is effectively hashed at 72 chars. This is a known bcrypt limitation—consider Argon2id if you need full-length support.

5. **Not re-evaluating cost annually.** OWASP recommends increasing the cost factor as hardware improves. A cost set in 2018 may be inadequate by 2026. Implement a version check in your auth flow to rehash on login when cost is below threshold.

faq.q: What is the bcrypt cost factor and what values are safe in 2026?
faq.a: The cost factor (also called the work factor or rounds parameter) is a **base-2 exponent** controlling how many key-expansion rounds bcrypt performs internally: cost N produces 2^N rounds. OWASP's 2025-2026 Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends a **minimum of cost=12** (~100 ms on a modern server CPU) for new deployments. Cost=13 (~200 ms) or cost=14 (~400 ms) provides stronger protection at the expense of longer login latency and slightly higher CPU cost per login. Anything below cost=12 is considered insufficient against modern GPU cracking rigs: cost=10 runs in ~12 ms on a CPU and is crackable at ~21,000 hashes/s on a single RTX 4090, which is too fast for a stolen hash database to be considered safe.

faq.q: How much does increasing the bcrypt cost by 1 affect hashing time?
faq.a: Each increment of 1 in the cost factor **exactly doubles** the hashing time, because the round count is 2^cost rather than a linear count. Going from cost=12 (~100 ms) to cost=13 means ~200 ms, cost=14 means ~400 ms, and cost=15 means ~800 ms. This exponential doubling applies **equally to defenders and attackers**: every +1 halves the attacker's brute-force throughput on the same hardware. This is what gives bcrypt its security: hardware improvements are matched by raising the cost factor over time, keeping the relative cost balance roughly constant for two decades.

faq.q: Why can't GPUs crack bcrypt as fast as they crack MD5 or SHA-256?
faq.a: bcrypt's Blowfish key schedule requires approximately **4 KB of working memory** per hash (the 18-element P-array plus four 256-element S-boxes of 32-bit words, all of which must be read and written on every round). GPU cores have very limited L1 cache per warp and thread, so when you try to parallelize bcrypt across thousands of GPU threads, the threads contend heavily for memory bandwidth and serialize, killing throughput. An NVIDIA RTX 4090 achieves roughly **164 billion MD5 hashes per second** but only **5,000-21,000 bcrypt hashes per second** depending on cost factor — a slowdown of about 10 million times. This memory-hardness is by deliberate design and is what makes bcrypt resilient against commodity GPU attackers.

faq.q: What is the 72-byte truncation limit in bcrypt and how does it affect security?
faq.a: The original bcrypt specification (Provos & Mazières, 1999) processes only the **first 72 bytes** of the password input. Any character beyond byte 72 is silently ignored. This means two passwords sharing the same first 72 bytes (for example, two passphrases with the same opening words) produce identical hashes. For typical passwords under 30 characters this is irrelevant, but it matters for long passphrases or for systems that allow arbitrary-length passwords without warning users. **Workarounds**: (1) pre-hash the password with SHA-512 before bcrypt to compress to 64 bytes (Dropbox's approach), but be careful about null bytes in the SHA-512 output; (2) switch to Argon2id, which has no truncation limit; or (3) enforce a 72-char maximum in your registration UI.

faq.q: How do I safely migrate a database from cost=10 to cost=12 without disrupting users?
faq.a: The standard approach is **opportunistic rehashing on login**. When a user authenticates successfully, your code: (1) verifies the password against the stored hash (which you can do regardless of cost), (2) checks whether the stored hash uses a cost lower than your current minimum (the cost factor is encoded in the hash itself: the `$2b$10$...` prefix indicates cost=10), (3) if so, rehashes the plaintext password (which you have momentarily in memory during the auth flow) at the new cost and updates the database record atomically. **No bulk migration is needed**: the upgrade happens passively as users log in over days, weeks or months. Users who don't log in remain at the old cost until they do; that's acceptable for inactive accounts, which face lower attack pressure anyway.

faq.q: Should I use bcrypt, Argon2id, or scrypt in 2026?
faq.a: **OWASP's 2025-2026 ranking puts Argon2id first**, followed by scrypt and then bcrypt. **Argon2id**, winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015), is memory-hard with **tunable memory AND time parameters** (typically 19 MiB and 2 iterations as a 2026 baseline), has no 72-byte truncation limit, and is more resistant to GPU/ASIC attacks. **scrypt** (Colin Percival, 2009) is also memory-hard and well-vetted. **bcrypt** is the oldest of the three and slightly weaker against GPUs, but is **universally supported across all languages and frameworks**, has 25+ years of cryptanalysis with no practical breaks, and is a pragmatic choice when Argon2id libraries are unavailable. **Never use** MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, plain SHA-512, or unsalted hashes for passwords — these are unsafe under any circumstance.

faq.q: How does bcrypt prevent rainbow-table attacks?
faq.a: bcrypt incorporates a cryptographic **salt**: a 128-bit random value generated independently per password at hashing time and stored alongside the resulting hash in the standard output format (`$2b$cost$22-char-salt$31-char-hash`). The salt is incorporated into the Blowfish key schedule, so even **two identical passwords produce completely different hashes**. A rainbow table precomputes hash→password mappings for a fixed hash function, but a unique salt invalidates any precomputed table: an attacker would need a separate rainbow table for **every possible 128-bit salt** (2^128 = 3.4 × 10^38 entries), which is computationally infeasible by many orders of magnitude. Salts make stolen hash databases force attackers into per-account brute-force, which is where bcrypt's slowness shines.

faq.q: What CPU/server specs should I benchmark bcrypt on before choosing a production cost?
faq.a: **Always benchmark on production hardware under expected load**, not a dev laptop. Key variables to consider: **CPU architecture** (ARM vs x86, server-grade vs consumer), **clock speed** under sustained load (Turbo Boost won't engage during high-concurrency hashing), **available cores dedicated to auth** (not contended by application threads), and whether CPU credits are **burstable** (AWS t-series CPU credits exhaust after sustained load, dropping you to baseline). A useful heuristic: pick the highest cost factor where time per hash stays under **250 ms on production hardware at peak concurrency**. For most cloud VMs with 2-4 vCPUs (AWS c-series, GCP n2, Azure D-series), cost=12 lands at ~80-150 ms per hash, a comfortable operating point. For ARM-based VMs (Graviton, Ampere), expect 2-3× slower than x86 at the same cost factor.

faq.q: What does a bcrypt hash actually look like and how do I parse the cost from it?
faq.a: A bcrypt hash is a 60-character ASCII string with the format `$2a$12$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy`. Decoded: `$2a$` (or `$2b$`, `$2y$`) is the **version identifier** (`2b` is the current canonical variant since 2014); `12$` is the **cost factor** (here, cost=12, encoded as a two-digit decimal); the next 22 characters are the **base64-encoded 128-bit salt**; the final 31 characters are the **base64-encoded 184-bit hash output**. To check the cost of a stored hash in code, parse positions 4-5 (the digits before the second `$`). Common library helpers (`bcrypt.getRounds()` in Node.js, `passlib.identify()` in Python, `password_get_info()` in PHP) abstract this for you.

faq.q: Is bcrypt vulnerable to timing attacks?
faq.a: **The hashing itself is not significantly vulnerable** because the computation time depends on the cost factor (chosen by you) and not on the password content; bcrypt's internal Blowfish key schedule does the same work regardless of password. However, the **comparison step** is critical: when you verify a login by comparing the computed hash against the stored hash, you must use a **constant-time comparison function** (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual()` in Node.js, `secrets.compare_digest()` in Python, `hash_equals()` in PHP), not a regular `==` or `strcmp` which short-circuits on the first byte difference. Most well-maintained bcrypt libraries use constant-time comparison internally, but if you implement your own verification logic, be careful. Also avoid measuring bcrypt latency over the network for unauthenticated endpoints — return a consistent response time.

faq.q: How often should I increase my bcrypt cost factor as hardware improves?
faq.a: **Roughly every 2-4 years, in line with Moore's Law and updates to OWASP's recommendation**. The historical progression: cost=8 was the standard around 2008-2012, cost=10 from 2012-2016, cost=12 from 2017-2026. As CPUs and GPUs get faster, what was once 'safe at 100 ms per hash' becomes faster on attacker hardware too. **Best practice**: build a periodic review (annual, tied to your security audit cycle) that compares your current minimum cost to the latest OWASP guidance. When OWASP raises the recommended minimum, update your application's bcrypt config and start opportunistic rehashing for existing users on next login. Do NOT bulk-rehash from cold storage; only do it during a user's authenticated session when you have the plaintext momentarily in memory.

faq.q: Can I use bcrypt for things other than password hashing, like API keys or tokens?
faq.a: **Generally no**, you should not use bcrypt (or any password-hashing function) for hashing API keys, session tokens, OAuth tokens, or other random secrets. Password-hashing functions are designed to be slow on purpose, to defend against brute-force of low-entropy human passwords. API keys and tokens are typically high-entropy random bytes (e.g., 256-bit) where brute-force is already infeasible against any reasonable hash function. For these use cases, a **fast cryptographic hash** like SHA-256 or SHA-512 (HMAC-SHA-256 if you have a server-side key) is appropriate and orders of magnitude faster. Reserve bcrypt and Argon2id specifically for user-chosen passwords.
